utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. I apologise for the late start. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. As scheduled, we'll have a housekeeping session to start with this morning, before we start with the case presentation by the Markac Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could beg the Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We have a preliminary issue that I think is important enough to raise before the MFI session, with the Court's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and can it be done in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We named our witnesses in May. We provided the Prosecution with a list of who our witnesses were going be and all the parties within the -- basically the first two weeks of our Defence case. We made a Rule 66 request in April, and again in May, and again in June, and again in October, and again in November. Our first Rule 66(B) disclosure that we received, I believe, was either last week or the Friday before last week. Last night, at 2.00 morning, we were notified that, of course, had I known I would have taken the cab from the -- from Amsterdam. I'm just joking. Had I known we would have obviously picked it up at 2.00 in the morning, but nobody was up at 2.00 in the morning. The documents in the Rule 66(B) disclosure that we received last night pertain to the witness -- one of the witnesses who will be testifying presumably today, if we are done with our first witness early enough. And it's -- as the Court is aware, we can't contact the witness once the witness has begun testifying. We have not been given the opportunity to look at these documents, to potentially discuss the documents with the witness who is coming to testify. Some of the documents, I have been just recently informed by my Case Manager, are documents that deal with VONS meetings in which our client -- or which our witness was present with President Tudjman among others. So it really puts us at a large disadvantage and quite frankly is unfair, and given the fact that the notice out there has been in existence for months, if not -- for weeks if not months, we are in a position in which we -- we are put a very difficult position with respect to this witness, and it is a very important witness. And he can only testify this week, and the Prosecution is aware that he can only testify this week. And we are -- we are at a loss to know what to do at this point, given the fact that this witness is probably going to testifying today. So I guess from my perspective, I don't want any of these documents showing up on a cross-examination list and being used in cross-examination because I think it is prejudicial to our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Obviously this is a huge disclosure obligation on us, and we try our best to comply with it. I think in relation to the second witness, the big one that might start today, there were more than 7.000 hits which are generated by the so-called ISU search. We review those, and the last batch apparently was disclosed last night. I'm fairly confident that the key exhibits that I'm going to use in cross-examination including the VONS meetings have been disclosed before. What this might be -- I'm not aware might be a translation or -- or something else, or duplication, but all the key exhibits that pertain to this witness were disclosed quite some time ago, and certainly not tonight. If this last batch of disclosure revealed a document for which, you know, the -- which is totally new and surprising to Defence, I'm sure we find a solution. Frankly, I haven't seen the 2.00 disclosure. I'm not sure what's on it. I'm happy to look at it, but I doubt that there is it anything which is -- which I'm going use in -- in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I rise because in addition to the issue of material being used in cross-examination by the Prosecution, there's also the issue, of course, of material that the Defence may feel is relevant and probative of certain issues in this trial that we haven't had an opportunity to review, to see if we wish to put it in because we think it has some significance to the trial even if the Prosecution perhaps doesn't. So, as far as I see from the disclosure list, we're talking about 118 documents that were disclosed to us at 2.00 this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kuzmanovic, you are talking about 66(B) disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. We made a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is any documents in the Prosecutor's custody or control which are material to the preparation of the Defence or are intended for use by the Prosecutor as evidence. And you'd say that once your list of witnesses was available to the Prosecution, they could have made up their mind what they want to use and what they do not want to use. Now, I do understand that the 118 documents were disclosed this night at 2.00 p.m. is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: 2.00 a.m., Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's not yet 2.00 p.m. Mr. Waespi, you say you're confident that it must be translations issues and the like and not really something material. Well, one of the things I do not fully understand is why in this and -- there are -- I have no problems in accepting that in this huge disclosure obligation that it is at 2.00 a.m., that is seven hours before the start of the hearing that day, that, at that moment, something is possible, which would not have been possible three days earlier. That's something I really do not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I mentioned before, this is a huge hit list in relation it this witness, and I have made available a lot of resources this week to comply with these disclosure issues, and a team of people worked over the weekend, and they finished their searches, and the Case Manager came in yesterday evening to review those searches, and -- and disclose it to the Defence. And as far as I know, there are still quite some materials which pertain to the Rule 66(B) request. These are all the public appearances of the second witness which is an enormous amount of materials. This is still ongoing and it might reveal some new documents again. Not documents I'm going use. Those have all been disclosed, which is unusual in fact. There is not one document on my list of cross-examination that has not been disclosed to the -- to the -- to Defence before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if -- I would have told my father such a story, I would have known his answer. He would have said, So you started too late?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are many, many witnesses which require an enormous amount of resources. We do our best do comply with these searches. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the other thing I wanted to add is we have received rolling disclosures. I think this was batch 6 of the disclosures, and the disclosures have all been placed on a CD in our locker which is fine if it's during the working day, or even if it's not, we can see the e-mail and go get it at our locker. But there isn't -- there is usually a spreadsheet on that CD which is easily e-mailable, so we could have at least looked through that to be able to -- to do that remotely. Every time there is a disclosure somebody has to haul off to the Tribunal, to the locker, to get the CD, so obviously at 2.00 a.m. it wasn't practical, but if somebody was up early enough, like our Case Manager was, he could have at least looked through the spreadsheet to see what was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the spreadsheet now available at least, so you've seen it by now? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have not but my Case Manager and co-counsel have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Waespi, one of the matters raised by Mr. Kuzmanovic was that he -- well, he's not allowed to have further contact with the witness once he has taken the stand. Would you allow for an exception in relation to these 118 documents, upon -- well, let's say, good cause being shown on the basis of the -- of the spreadsheet, that it would be unreasonable not to allow Mr. Kuzmanovic to discuss some of these documents with -- with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, I have no problem with that. Can I just make another point, in relation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before -- this was a quick answer. Mr. Kuzmanovic, would that -- of course, that requires a quite a bit of self-discipline. Do you think that this would, at least to some extent, create not a solution but at least some relief?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would. I think that's a reasonable solution. It all really depends on how quickly we can get through the documents and obviously, as officers of the court, we will let the Court know that the only things we would talk about with the witness are these new documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and nothing else under those circumstances. Mr. Waespi, you would like to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just two points in relation to disclosure. As you know, there is a huge Rule 68 disclosure ongoing in relation to the Cermak Defence which ties up a lot of resources from our side as well, and they have reminded us, rightly so, I think a week ago, that we should speed that up process. Second, we asked Markac Defence in relation to the second witness, to which this disclosure relates to, to move him up, because we knew that it's going to be massive disclosure, and unfortunately, as Mr. Kuzmanovic pointed out, the witness is so busy that we couldn't move him back. But we tried to, as we always do, to accommodate each other's schedule but it was not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that goodwill apparently is there but that does not always create results which are workable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I mean, we are in -- Mr. Waespi and the Defence are in constant contact via e-mail and during the breaks about things that were coming up with respect to our case, and it's not that we are accusing the Prosecution of doing this deliberately. We're not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's -- you know, the other issue that we have with respect to the relief that the Court has in mind for us is that we have to look at these documents, read them and analyse them. They are not just four- or five-page documents. You know, some of these documents are 20, 30 pages long. Some of them don't have translations. So it takes us a little bit longer. But we will -- maybe when -- after the first break we can let the Court know how long it might take to us look and analyse these documents before we can really say whether that relief that the Court is thinking of is even practical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would it be an idea -- Mr. Waespi was quite clear on -- he was quite confident that likely most of this material was already disclosed once. He must have good reasons for that and he could share those reasons so that it might be easier for you to find out whether this material has been disclosed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm mainly talking about the VONS meetings. These are key documents and I would be surprised if a totally new VONS meeting document was disclosed last night, but I might be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see. Mr. Waespi, if -- there must have been reasons why these 118 documents were selected for further disclosure, which means that they had not been disclosed previously or not exactly in the same format or whatever. Well, the one who -- the one who decided that, or at least the one who selected those documents as still to be disclosed, must have had an idea on why these documents needed to be disclosed and perhaps that knowledge could assist Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. There is basically the result of the Rule 66(B) request to have documents in which the witness appears. These are numerous press conferences, and I'm quite sure many of them relate to these public appearances of this witness, and -- but the VONS meeting apparently, you know, catch the eye of Mr. Kuzmanovic and that's an important document. And -- and all the other documents, as I say, are numerous documents which recall public appearances of witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is more or less rumble for you than -- rather than -- yes. At the same time, we know that sometimes public appearance can provide important information. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is exactly the point, I guess. You know, we don't have the database that the OTP has, and the whole reason for Rule 66(B) was to enable to us be able to find some of that information that either is not in the public domain, is not in any of our databases, or -- I mean, that is the whole purpose of that disclosure and the request for the disclosure. So we will -- we will look at this obviously during the first break. We will consult with Mr. Waespi and then we will let the Court know, if that is okay with the Court, what we -- what we would recommend to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just to correct the record. That's the only reason I rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The overwhelming majority of these documents actually appear to be presidential transcripts. From just a quick scroll through them, I would say at least 70 per cent of them, and therefore, if they're of the length of a typical presidential transcript, these are probably at least 50 pages long in the original, so they are quite a bit of work to review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then, of course, we have seen some presidential transcript but, of course, I have got no idea whether there are any new ones among them. Mr. Waespi, could you please pay attention to that as well to what extent presidential transcripts are new.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, one last request. I realise, and I don't know how practical it is, but I would ask if there are further disclosures, that at least the spreadsheet get e-mailed to us if that is possible, and then we'll obviously look through that and be able to determine whether it's something that we need to review right away and get from the locker or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Waespi, may I take it that before further disclosure takes place, that always, immediately, a spreadsheet will be sent to the Defence so that what they find on the CD doesn't come as a surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm afraid that the Chamber, I'm looking at the parties, apart from taking notice of this at this moment, before you have had an opportunity to look at it, I think it would be -- it would be too early to make any drastic decisions based on the submissions and observations until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I agree with Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Misetic, in view of your observations in relation to material -- documents material to the preparation of the Defence, I take it that when -- once have you seen this list, and if there are any further observations to be made, that you will make them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will then start with the housekeeping session. The first one I would like to deal with on my list is D1569, if I could say the famous Goran and -- Goran Vunic documents. One of the things that's still missing, Mr. Waespi, is what the position of the Prosecution is in relation to these documents, and you will certainly remember that we're talking about authenticity and names being in there or another name being in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier will deal with the matter. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Yes, I think the Prosecution's position was similar to your own position when the issue came up, which was whether or not authenticity attested to by another person who is not testifying, who isn't here, who's not been cross-examined, is sufficient in order to authenticate the document. So the Prosecution takes the same position whether that's a proper way of doing it. The document in question, I understand, didn't have a stamp on it and that's where the issue arose, but other than that, the Prosecution doesn't have any other position on those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further submissions in response to what Mr. Carrier says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just with regard to this document, Mr. President, the concerns expressed by the Prosecution simply go to the weight of the document, not to its admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think there's hardly any risk that if D1569 is admitted into evidence, that not only immediately all alarm bells will be ringing when we see this document also in comparison to other --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- documents, that's P1063 and D918. Then, under those circumstances, the Chamber decides that D1569 is admitted into evidence. Then we move on to D1669, D1670, D1671, and D1672. Let me just have a look; one second, please. These are all bar tabled housing law documents. One of the matters was that these bar tabled documents that the Chamber was still waiting for the filing of -- the joint filing of a -- by the parties, this being a bar table document which is in need of a spreadsheet, in which relevance, et cetera, and any observations are laid down. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. My understanding is that these documents are going to be dealt with on Friday in the -- in the joint bar table submission. As you just said. But I don't think there's much point in going through it out now other than -- because in the bar table submission will a column with Defence position and another column with the Prosecution's position, so it should be laid out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that will be filed. I do understand that such a spreadsheet will not be evidence but just serves as guidance for the Chamber. So, therefore, we would like to know -- that joint filing apparently is not yet prepared or is not -- the filing is not there yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just correct that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is my understanding from my Case Manager that these specific documents will not be part of the joint filing. It's my understanding the joint filing deals with documents from the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The ones in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We have circulated a new proposed bar table, which we have submitted only to the Prosecution and the parties at this point, which contains the Vaganj, the housing law, and certain other documents which we will then all put into one filing for the Chamber and -- and file. So all of that will be in the filing that deals with new bar table documents which we are going bar table into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because what we now need is a -- the Chamber has to decide on -- I just mentioned four documents, which are, from what I understand, all housing -- I see one is Housing Act, Official Gazette number 51. Law on Modification of the Law on Housing, Official Gazette number 42. Law on Changes and Amendments to the Law on Housing, Official Gazette number 22 of 1992, I think, Article 2. And the Official Gazette number 70, Law on Amendments to the Law on Housing. These are the documents I just referred to. Now, we expect a filing, a spreadsheet filing, a joint filing by the parties on relevance, et cetera, as we have explained before. Now, for those documents that were already admitted into evidence we expect this new, could I say, consolidated filing giving all this information, not to be evidence but as guidance for the Chamber. Now, should we now admit these documents already before we have received these new four ones where we have not yet received a submission, joint filing, spreadsheet, in relation to these documents or should we wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would propose that we clear the MFI list because I assure the Court, and the Prosecution has received a copy of our proposed submission, we have the comments from the Prosecution actually on the bar on the housing laws. If necessary, if you wish, we can do a separate filing today and just file that on the bar table because it is already done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we will do, we'll then clear our MFI list by deciding on admission. But, at the same time, we'll add to the pending issues list, the issue of still needing a spreadsheet in relation to these four documents, or if there are more, then we'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then under those circumstances, D1669, D1670, D1671, and D1672 are admitted into evidence. And I put clearly on the record, that the Chamber expects, could the parties commit themselves to a date?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, I believe we've already put our comments and we had no objections so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As I indicated, Mr. President, the actual housing law bar table is ready and we could file it today if necessary. However, last week we sent that as part of a larger bar table proposal which is still with the Prosecution, and we're waiting for the Prosecution's comments on other documents. I think it would be more efficient if we just made one filing where everything was on it, but if the Chamber prefers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps since we have now dealt specifically with these four documents, that we separate them from the others, that it is clear that by this Wednesday --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Today. Today. We'll file it today, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll file it today so that we have the spreadsheet information, joint filing, today on these documents. Then I move to D1684. There's no issue about admission. The main -- the only remaining matter seems to be whether the -- now the relevant portion has been uploaded in e-court so that we are not stuck with a huge document, whereas it is only intended that portions of it are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the excerpts that were used with Witness Rincic have been uploaded as 65 ter 1D2979. The Court Officer has linked this already to D1684, and it is ready to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could confirm this, the Chamber is ready to decide.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1684 is admitted into evidence. I now move to D1717, which is a video of a concert. I think we've seen 17 seconds, and the parties were invited to agree on what songs were and what songs were not sung. And I do understand that even for the short clip shown that there was an objection, because it lacked relevance. An objection by the Prosecution. Could I hear from the -- from the parties. And it's mainly about what was not sung during the remainder of the concert.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll just start, Mr. President. This was something that was addressed during the evidence of Mr. Pasic. And during his testimony he said he wasn't actually there, number one. So he wouldn't be in a position to say what was sung or wasn't sung for the reminder of. What's on the video itself, the Prosecution's position is that's not a complete record of what transpired during the concert. It ends rather abruptly. It doesn't contain the entire concert, so to -- for the Prosecution to be in a position to say what was not or was sung during the entire concert, obviously we're not in a position to do that. We have video. We have watched the video. We can say what was and what was not sung on the video itself, but in terms of concert, you -- it is impossible seeing a little piece of something to say, Well, therefore, because nothing is in that video-clip, it couldn't have been happening off camera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I do understand that if the parties agree that on the video-clip that no Ustasha songs were sung that, of course, is not a guarantee to say that perhaps someone in the audience may have whispered some Ustasha songs. Of course, what the Chamber wanted to avoid is that we have to look at the two-hour video, then we would need to have all the songs translated and then, at the end, to find out that no Ustasha songs were sung. That's not the way in which the Chamber wants to spend their days and therefore the parties invited to check and to see whether they could agree on whether any Ustasha songs during this concert as shown in the video were sung. That is the issue. Have the parties looked at it, have they made up their mind, have they tried to reach agreement on whether what they saw and what they heard, whether there were any Ustasha songs. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think there is agreement that there are no Ustasha songs on this video. I am unaware of the reference to this being a partial video. As Your Honour has indicated, it is a two-hour video --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then let's be -- Mr. Pasic may not have seen it all. What we have is the video. Of course, we could try -- we could advertise and invite people who have seen parts of the concert which were not shown on the video and then distribute the video among half of the population of the Croatia in order to find out whether anyone has heard anything which does not appear in that video. That is, of course, not the way in which we would like to proceed. Have the parties agreed on whether, as shown on the video, this concert, whether there's any reason for the Chamber to look at it, because Ustasha songs would be -- would have been sung. That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: As I said, on the basis of what's on the video itself, the Prosecution is in a position so say there are no Ustasha songs sung on the video. That is not to say that no Ustasha songs were sung during that concert. Again, the video ends --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: -- abruptly, and so we're not in a position to say whether or not it goes on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, did I not yet address that matter a second ago? You just repeat what you said. Therefore, there seems to be no need for the Chamber to look at this video. There has been a concert, whether fully recorded or not is the second matter, but from the available recording of that concert the parties agree it does not show or produce any Ustasha songs. Is that in agreement? Is there agreement on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And there's one other point just with respect to that video and I think it is agreed, but if it is agreed, then there is no need for the Chamber to look at the video. But that is the -- Mr. Pasic testified that the concert involved two opera singers named Matic and Cigoj, and the other relevance of this video is that Mr. Matic and Mr. Cigoj are on this video, at a concert in Knin, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But for that purpose I think we looked at 17 seconds only or something like that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and that would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that then one saves 1 hour, 59 minutes, and 43 seconds. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'm not going to repeat myself, but given the Mr. Pasic wasn't there, perhaps the -- if it is going to be admitted, that description of the document be changed where it says he was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have for D1717, as a description, "Video of concert in Knin castle." Nothing more, nothing less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. President, there is a different one on the MFI list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- but I will make sure that the one that's on the MFI list matches the one that's with you, which is just a general description.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, any further objections, then, or -- if this is done?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The portion uploaded, is that the portion shown or is there anything more in it, Mr. Registrar? As far as you are ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is not clear from the date in e-court whether that is a full clip or just what was shown in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the parties inform the Chamber, whether we have 17 seconds or two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We're checking on that right now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if it is two hours, you perhaps could already reduce it to 17 seconds. I'll move on to D1719, and I already indicate that the Chamber will not decide on admission at this moment. However, this document, which is -- if I could briefly describe it as the Jarnjak interview. Mr. Misetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could perhaps state our position. Having reviewed it, I think we're satisfied that the relevant portions of this video were put on the transcript for purposes of impeachment, and therefore, we no longer feel the need to move this into evidence. Unless the Chamber feels the need to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said before, the Chamber will not -- I earlier said that the Chamber would not decide on admission. You say, Well, we don't need it anymore. So then the remaining position question is whether the Prosecution and/or the Chamber think that this material is such that it should be received in evidence. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No, our position is it should not be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it is only the Chamber will have to consider whether or not we can do without.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I also have an answer for D1717, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you just allow me to visit first D1719. The Defence has withdrawn this from its tendering. Mr. Carrier doesn't seek it to be admitted into evidence. It keeps the MFI status for the time being, until the Chamber has decided whether the Chamber would like to have this document in evidence and will call upon the producing party to produce it. I would say to tender it. Otherwise, of course, the Chamber always has the possibility to make it a Chamber exhibit. But, for the time being, D1719 keeps the status of a document marked for identification. D1717, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I understand that in e-court is actually a list of all the songs that were sung. My Case Manager advises me that we have both a short clip of the 17 seconds ready and the entire two-hour concert ready, and it is simply up to the Chamber which clip you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, what songs were sung, once the parties have agreed that these are no Ustasha songs, then we do not have to know the whole programme. Is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, I suggest, and I will hear from Mr. Carrier whether he agrees or not, that we keep it to the 17-seconds video even without the list, which would be good musical education but not assist the Chamber in deciding matters it has to decide. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Just with respect to the list itself, it's not something that I'm positive that we have had a chance to review the list. So I understand what Your Honour is saying, but if the list is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you agree that no Ustasha songs were sung, what's the use of going through the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: To look at the list and see what the actual list consists of because I want to make sure that the list actually corresponds to what was on the videos. Simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would say there is a possibility that you'd find on the list Ustasha songs which are not shown on the video and that would then meet your concerns that the video might not be show nasty songs which, nevertheless, may have been performed at the concert. Is that -- I'm trying understand your reasoning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: My reasoning is simply is just to -- out of an abundance of caution just to look at the list and see what's on the list. Having not seen it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if is not evidence, what would be your concern?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: That's fine. That was the only concern, that it go into evidence or not go into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I suggested that we do not have to know the full programme of the concert if the parties agree that no Ustasha songs were sung, and that who has a beard and who has no beard, and who is singing, we can look at that 17 seconds. The Gotovina Defence is invited to upload the 17-seconds version, and to -- if it was uploaded, the list, to strike that, so that the only thing that then remains is the 17-seconds video, not for the music sung but mainly for the presence of persons on that video, and Mr. Pasic, I think, testified about that, and was not in agreement with those who organised the concert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We will do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then -- could you inform the Registrar once this is done. D1717, being a 17-second video-clip as shown to the witness Petar Pasic, is admitted into evidence. If there's any problem with the uploading of this document, the Registrar and the Chamber should be informed immediately. Then we move on. D1728. That was a bar table submission which the Chamber had not seen at the time. It was tendered. There were no objections. The Chamber meanwhile has read the document and D1728 is admitted into evidence. We move on to D1784. We first had a document, the expert report of Mr. Deverell. Then the -- what was found in the corrigendum was worked in, in the original document. There was a second corrigendum and there was a problem with the page references. That was the problem at the time. Then later, during the testimony of Mr. Deverell, the Cermak Defence agreed -- agreed that the portion on the Grubori document that was still remaining in the report, so not the part that was already taken out before the report was presented but what remains in the report would then be taken out as well. I don't remember exactly. It was, I think, page 53 or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Page 55, Your Honour, lines 17 to 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have we now a document uploaded in which all the corrections, including the corrections to the page references and this page 55 has worked -- has been worked in so that there's a final version which meets in every respect what should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour. We have done exactly as we agreed with the Prosecution, as the Court requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then there was no further objections. So, under those circumstances, D1784, as uploaded now, is admitted into evidence. Then I move on to D1686. This all started, I think, with the HINA report. Then we had additional information from the Helsinki Watch web site. And then later, the parties were provided with additional material Mr. Skegro had been provided. Now the Chamber has not looked at that material because we found it appropriate that the parties would say have it and would consider what they want to tender, and I -- when I'm talking about D1686, we should keep in mind that it is related to P2642, which is a report regarding the media situation in Croatia. The Chamber wonders what the parties would like to have in evidence so that a -- that balanced information or -- as complete as possible information is available to the Chamber, or whether they would say, The less the Chamber knows about it, the better it is. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We would seek the admission of D1686 into evidence for the very reason that you said Your Honour, in order to provide a balanced picture to the Court. There was an issue of the translation of that document. I think you will recall that it had to be read into the record because we only took it off the web site as we were going along. But a translation of that document has now been produced and has been uploaded, and we would therefore seek admission of it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the portion from the Helsinki Watch web site was exhibited, if I'm not mistaken. And then what then remains are the judgements, Croatian judgements provided by the witness, once he had left this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any reason to have them in evidence as well, which might be good to complete the picture, because I do understand that the judgement may give some better insight on what has happened and what has not happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think we are still waiting to receive those from him, but I can certainly follow that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, my information at this moment is that some material was sent by Mr. Skegro, that it was received by the Chamber but made available to the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said before, the Chamber considered it not that it for us to decide what was in evidence, but rather, to make it available to the parties to see, check relevance and to see whether they wished to tender any of that material. I immediately add to that, that since there was a matter of accusations which were then denied, that, if judgements were rendered in this respect, that it might complete the picture so as to know whether there's anything relevant in it or that we could just forget about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, if it has been transmitted to us, Your Honour, I was unaware of that, but I'm sure it has been, and we will get on to it and check it and then come back to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at the Prosecution. Could you confirm that you have received it, because ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And of course, I can imagine that D1686 does not immediately trigger your attention for material which was sent but is not to be found under number D1686, which is just the HINA report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, my understanding is we did receive the judgements. They haven't been translated. However, perhaps if I could just have an opportunity just to make a few comments on P2642, which ties in, obviously, to everything else. But I think that document served as the good-faith basis to put a certain question and then it basically ran its course. The Prosecution's position is that none of that needs to actually become exhibited in the case which would mean that P2642, D1686 -- and then there no need to go through the translations of the judgements. The question was asked, it was answered, and the Prosecution is satisfied with leaving it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber will consider it, but the Chamber might want or might -- might be inclined to say that if we heard a beginning of a story, then another part of a story which may be half of the story or three-quarters of the story or 20 per cent of the -- 25 per cent of the story, that if there is material which would complete our view on the matter, that we would then like to see that as well, and not -- because I did understand from the witness, but, please, I don't know whether my recollection is complete in that respect, something had happened, although not what he was charged with. Now, under those circumstances, what has happened, I do not know whether in this judgement anything is established about that. But to have a complete picture, to see whether we can just forget about all of it or whether, well, 5 or 10 per cent remains. That may be possible on the basis of these judgements. I do even understand that he sent even more material than he announced in court. So we leave that open at this moment. But your suggestion is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can be more complete now. Mr. Skegro has sent material in files named P1, P2, P3, P4, R1, and T1; six documents. The P documents stand for criminal verdict; the R stands for - and I'm certain that I'll pronounce it wrongly - "rjesenje" which is a Croatian word for "decision," from what I understand; and the T documents stands for "tuzba" which is explained as a Croatian word for "private criminal indictment." The first -- the four P documents refer to, as Mr. Skegro calls it, the pistol story; R1 and T1 refer to the stolen money story. This material, which was sent electronically, has been forwarded by our Registrar on the 7th of October in the early afternoon. "The parties are invite by the Trial Chamber to review these documents and consider whether or not to tender them into evidence. Furthermore," Mr. Registrar reports to the parties, "I have been asked to inform the parties that the Trial Chamber, not having reviewed the material itself and having been briefed on the contents only very superficially, reserves its position in respect of the use of its discretion under Rule 98." That is more or less what I earlier said today. The parties are invited to review that material and to see whether there's any wish to tender it. If so, then, of course, translations will be made. The Chamber will consider it. If the parties would decide that they have no interest whatsoever, then the Chamber would still consider whether this material, which was send by Mr. Skegro at the request of the Chamber, whether we want to use our discretion under Rule 98. So we will hear from the parties. At the same time, at this moment, D1686 and D20 -- P2642, any mutual objections or ... Of course, when talking about the D documents, any objections from the Prosecution and/or any objections against the P documents by the Defence? No objections. Then D1686 and P2642 are admitted into evidence. I move on to P2640, minutes of a presidential meeting, 11th of April 1995. The Cermak Defence would consider what portion of this relatively large document of 120 pages would be needed to create a proper context for the portion which got specific attention during the evidence of Mr. Skegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I believe that we've already informed the Prosecution and are waiting to hear from them on that issue. It was simply putting the original part that the Prosecution were relying into some form of context, and I think the same applies to the next exhibit. But certainly if they've not yet made a decision on that, we can discuss it. It --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the Chamber was more or less waiting for an agreement on the selection and there also was some --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There was a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- translation issue there as well. So the Chamber was wondering whether any agreement had been reached by the parties on this, so that we could have the relevant portion uploaded with the right translation and then decide on admission. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, with respect to the context issue for P2640, as well as P2641, I think that has been resolved, and there's agreement between the parties with respect to that. Your Honour is correct. There is a second issue with regard to the translation. My understanding is that that was sent to the Registry; however, we're still waiting for a response. We have requested a final translation. Just hasn't come back. So we're still waiting for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Carrier, you say, The matter is resolved, we have agreement with the Cayley Defence -- with the Cermak Defence, with Mr. Cayley. From his words, it was not obvious that he was aware of the agreement. He made a proposal, apparently. You did not disagree. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What I -- Mr. Carrier's recollection may be better than mine. All I recall is we certainly gave the pages that we requested that should be included and I don't think there was any other proposal, and if Mr. Carrier's saying that he agrees to that, then yes, we're in agreement. I can clarify the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's then -- then the translation issue remains. I then suggest that we -- at this moment that we keep the status of P2640 as an MFI, but only in view of the translation. And the Cermak Defence is invited to upload exclusively, perhaps apart from the cover page, which indicates what the document is about, but as far as the substance is concerned, only those pages and remove everything else, so that the only matter that then remains is translation. Mr. Cayley, if that -- it has not yet been done, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, I don't think it has, Your Honour, but we'll certainly do it. And I will speak to Mr. Carrier in the break so that we can make sure it gets down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then finally, translation to be dealt with as soon as possible. P2641, minutes of a VONS meeting, same problem. But no translation issue, apparently. Only a selection, a portion to be selected. Agreement there as well. Not yet uploaded?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then P2641 is admitted into evidence. The section that has been selected and on which selection the parties have agreed for purposes of context. If the selected portion is not uploaded within the next 48 hours, the Chamber wants to be informed and, of course, the Registrar should be informed about that. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise, there might be some confusion because Mr. Cayley likely was dealing with Mr. Hedaraly on this issue. I have a note from Mr. Hedaraly to the effect that both of the contextual portions of the transcript have been uploaded, but perhaps Mr. Cayley can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I would need to check, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's like in one of the plays of Moliere, where Mr. Jourdain says, I didn't know that I've spoke in prose for the whole of my life already. Mr. Cayley, you are now been informed about what you have done in your past. That doesn't change anything, that P2640 is a still an MFI awaiting the settling of the translation issue. And that P2641 is admitted into evidence. We move on to P2643. That is an article in "The Independent" publication on Tudjman tapes, 1st of November, 2000. This is a document, in relation to which Mr. Skegro has sent us the R and the T document. This also has been provided to the parties. The -- here, again, it may be wise to wait until the parties have looked at this T and this R document, so as to know what additional light it sheds on the testimony of Mr. Skegro. Also, because I think he testified that it would have been better to look at the original rather than at any publication on the conversation which was reported in P2643. Could I urge the parties to make up their mind, both in relation to the P documents and on this T and R document as well so that we would hear no later than, well, let's say by the end of this week, what the parties intend to do with it. Even if there is no full translation yet ready, I may take it that both parties will have an opportunity to look at these documents as to find out perhaps on a more superficial level what they are about and whether they want to use them, yes or no, and then, of course, if they will be tendered into evidence, then we would need a formal translation. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I hesitate only because we have not been disclosed, as far as I know, the underlying transcript of the conversation at issue in P2643.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it exists. Of course, Mr. Skegro suggested that it would be better to look at that. Whether it is there or not, I do not know. But perhaps Mr. Carrier can inform us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: We are actually in the midst of trying to obtain that underlying document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To obtain it, which means that you don't have it. You're not trying to find it, or are you trying to?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: We don't have it. We are trying to get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic -- Mr. Carrier, is there any expectation as far as when -- whether it is likely that you will receive it, and if so, when you would receive it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I can't advise. We asked for it some time ago and then there was a bit of a problem in obtaining it, so at the moment I just don't know when it is going to comment, if it exists. I don't know anything other than we've asked and we've made another request, and we still haven't received it, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the transcript is allegedly cited in -- it is cited, I should say, in the article itself so I would assume that that indicates that it does exist. If it now doesn't exist, then that would, I think, go to the admissibility of this document. So, we would reserve until we actually get the chance to see the underlying transcript because the witness seemed to dispute the description of the underlying conversation, and I think in fairness to the witness and parties, we should be able to assess and put into context whatever was discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think he said there was nothing illegal in the matters that were discussed and that we could see that from the original of the transcript. Now, of course, if you say, It's quoted; therefore, it does exist, it suggests that, at least at the time, it did exist. And I have sometimes, in my life - I'm not saying in this case - I have seen quotes of documents that have never existed at all which were just false quotes. So it is an open matter. I would say that we would look at this, also in relation to the T and the R documents you'll still review. It may be that it will shed some additional light on the matter or not. It seems not to be a key issue in this case. Therefore, the parties are invited to make up their minds, as far as matters stand now, on the basis of the material which is available, and we are all aware that there may be other material, that is, the transcripts themselves, still to come, but that's not certain. Then, under those circumstances, P2643 keeps the status of a document marked for identification. The last one on my list is P2644. We are awaiting -- we were waiting for a new translation. Is the new translation there and uploaded? There were no objections against the document as such. It's a P document, so I would expect a document -- expect an answer from the Prosecution. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, I understand there was a translation issue raised by the Gotovina Defence. I'm not sure whether or not it has been corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you find that out in the next break, and inform the Chamber, I would say, within 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, apparently -- I have just received a note saying it has not been dealt with yet. It was sent to be reviewed, as I understand, and there's been no response to that yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No response to that yet. Could you try to find out, since it is a document which is, apart from the translation issue, ready for admission, under what -- with what urgency the matter can be dealt with by CLSS. Then the last matter on my list is that it was brought to the Chamber's attention that D896 seems to be a duplicate of D629 -- D625. I've not personally checked that. If it is correct, D896 should be vacated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we can just check on the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would be so kind to do that, Mr. Kehoe. I think that I went through what I found on my MFI list. Any other matter to be raised?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are two matters which I would like to briefly raise. First, in relation to the Cermak Defence, still there were ongoing talks on agreement on the basis of the Milosevic and Martic material. Apart from the disclosure which was kept separate. Has that resulted yet in ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think those talks are still ongoing, as far as I understand it. I'm not actually involved in those talks on the team. I think Mr. Waespi ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that relates to the -- we received a draft filing on Friday and, just before court, discussed it with Mr. Cayley, and I think can be signed today. It's basically a notice to the Trial Chamber, if the Defence agrees about agreed facts, plus a map that shows where these facts took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's be very practical. Mr. Waespi, you are confident that it could be filed today, because, apparently, you agreed with the suggestions made. If not, within the next 48 hours a -- it would then be a joint filing, I take it, agreed facts, the joint filing. If it's not being filed within the next 48 hours, the Chamber would expect you to revisit the matter and to take initiative to that in court. Then, finally, we have the famous outstanding matter of "fire" or "strike." D970 compared to P1272. The word "udari." Mr. Misetic, could I hear from you? I do understand that you have submitted the matter to CLSS and that they informed you that there was no reason to translate the word in a different way as they had done. And if I'm -- it was "strike" rather than "fire," is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would have to look back quickly at my e-mail communications here. But what happened is, we submitted that sentence to CLSS. They agreed that it needed to be changed and made a change to say, Put the towns, et cetera, under artillery fire. We then went back and said, There's another document in evidence where the same word "udar" is translated as "strike" and not "fire," and we believe that for the sake of consistency of the two documents that the word should be translated the same. Our suggestion was "strike," but if is "fire" in both or "strike" in both, just as long as it is translated the same way. Their response back was that they wouldn't translate it -- change the translation because it was a faithful translation of the word "udar" in the second, meaning in D970, and therefore they refused to change it. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that the result is that we have still the same word translated differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... different ways, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In two different ways. Of course, I'm not familiar with the reasons. Is this context, is this any grammatical -- well, whatever it is. Would you like the Chamber to ask for further explanation --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and more an explanation which goes into the details of why in the one context the one translation is used and in the other context another word apparently has been used. Is that what you would like the Chamber to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have tried that myself already and have not received a response, and therefore I would ask the Chamber if -- to make an inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the inquiry would then seek a -- well, as an expert explanation on the use of the different words, where the original, although I think, but the one is "udari" and the other is "udar," but I take it that may be a matter of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Singular and plural.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Why in the one translation the one word has been chosen and why in the other translation the other word has been chosen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would have any suggestions as to how to formulate such a question, the Chamber would like to receive it within 24 hours. If you have no further detailed suggestion, that's not a long list of matters to be raised but that the most -- the sharpest way in formulating that question, if we do not receive anything from you, of course, then the Chamber will do it itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further matters on my list. Any of the parties? If not -- yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just very quickly, Your Honour, so we can move straight on to the witness. I've checked D896 and D625. They are indeed complete duplicates. They're our documents, so one of them can be vacated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then we will vacate the second one that you -- if you give me a minute. D896 is vacated. If there is no further matter, we'll have a break, and we will resume at five minutes past 11.00, and -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of the time estimates given for the first witness in the Markac Defence, the Chamber will not, at this moment, further deal with the disclosure issue raised before the break, because there's not much of a chance that we would start the second witness today, and this gives the parties a bit more time so that we could communicate on the matter this afternoon, if need be, unless there's any such urgent matter that we would have to hear about immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think what we'll do is, obviously if we do not get through with this witness, or do by the end of the day, we will have time today and we'll address it tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Then, this is the moment where the Markac Defence will start its case presentation. And we'll hear the testimony of the first witness the Markac Defence will present. Before, however, we start hearing that evidence, the Chamber would like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We started hearing the case presentation of the Markac Defence this morning in closed session. The reasons for turning into closed session will be put on the record at a later stage. We adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 17th of November, 9.00 in this same courtroom, III. And just as information for the public, we expect that we would go into closed session immediately after the case has been called for unknown period of time. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of November, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.52 p.m.,
